records.claim: Jung describes archetypes as structural patterns of the collective unconscious that shape recurrent forms of imagination, symbolism and behavior.
The collective unconscious is distinguished from the personal unconscious and is proposed as a deeper layer of psychic structure common to human beings.
Archetypal contents typically become available to consciousness through symbolic images, myths, dreams and fantasies rather than as literal propositions.
The mother archetype is treated as a recurring symbolic pattern with multiple manifestations rather than as a single biographical image.
The anima concept is used to describe a structured unconscious figure associated with the male psyche in Jung's model.
Jung connects awareness of unconscious contents with individuation, a process of differentiating and integrating aspects of the psyche.
Unconscious archetypal contents can be projected onto people or external objects, making their psychic origin harder to recognize.
Psychological development involves an ongoing relation between conscious awareness and unconscious processes rather than total identification with either.
Mythological motifs are treated as culturally variable expressions of recurring psychic patterns.
Archetypal patterns can persist across historical change while taking different symbolic forms in particular cultures.
The archetype theory is a depth-psychological framework and should not be silently converted into a claim that archetypes are experimentally verified universal neural modules.
The collective unconscious is conceptually distinct from a social archive or simple inherited memory of specific events.
The source is most useful for comparative analysis when symbolic phenomenology, psychological interpretation and ontological claims are coded separately.
Aion centers on the phenomenology of the Self and its relation to conscious ego identity.
The shadow represents relatively unconscious aspects of personality that can be encountered through self-observation and projection.
Anima and animus are treated as archetypal structures whose projections can strongly shape interpersonal experience.
Recognition of projection is part of the process through which unconscious material can become psychologically differentiated.
Jung explicitly situates the shadow, anima and animus within his account of the collective unconscious.
The Self is broader than the conscious ego and is used to represent a more comprehensive organization of psyche.
Integration of shadow material is described as an early movement in individuation and further development of the personality.
Psychological growth occurs partly through recognizing how inner structures shape one's relations with other people.
Archetypal structures are not identical to conscious self-concepts or deliberate beliefs.
Aion places psychic development within historical and symbolic patterns that recur across periods.
Aion is a Jungian psychological and symbolic framework, not a demonstrated account of universal neural architecture.
Individuation requires transformation in the relation between conscious identity and unconscious material rather than simple accumulation of information.
The text supports coding shadow, projection, anima/animus and Self as distinct motifs rather than collapsing them into a single 'unconscious' category.
Jung interprets alchemical coniunctio imagery as a symbolic representation of the union of psychological opposites.
The work analyzes paired opposites such as masculine/feminine, spirit/soul and conscious/unconscious as central symbolic structures.
The union of opposites is related to the emergence of a more complete sense of Self and psychic wholeness.
Alchemy is read psychologically, with its procedures and substances treated as projections of inner processes.
The conjunction is compared with stages of individuation in which previously separated aspects of personality are brought into relation.
Alchemical death-and-rebirth symbolism is interpreted as a model for psychological transformation.
The work explores symbolic relations between body and soul and the need to integrate rather than simply suppress their difference.
Jung emphasizes paradoxical images that hold opposed qualities together rather than reducing them to one side.
The alchemical symbols are interpreted as expressions of dynamics between consciousness and unconsciousness.
Integration is linked with self-knowledge and a more comprehensive relation to one's psychic totality.
These readings are Jung's psychological interpretations of alchemical symbolism, not evidence that historical alchemists experimentally discovered a modern psychology.
The coniunctio is treated as a transformation toward greater psychic wholeness rather than a static state.
The corpus should keep the historical alchemical source material distinct from Jung's later psychological interpretation of it.
Jung defines synchronicity as an acausal connecting principle involving meaningful coincidence.
The concept focuses on the meaningful relation experienced between events rather than only on their ordinary efficient causation.
Synchronicity is explicitly distinguished from a conventional causal mechanism linking one event materially to another.
Jung examines coincidences in which an inner psychological state and an external event appear meaningfully related.
Archetypal patterns are used as part of Jung's interpretation of why certain coincidences can carry unusual psychological meaning.
The significance of coincidence depends on temporal correspondence between otherwise apparently unrelated events.
The work discusses probability and exceptional coincidence as part of the problem of distinguishing meaningful pattern from chance.
Jung includes an experimental discussion of astrology as part of his historical and empirical exploration of synchronicity.
The book was published together with Wolfgang Pauli's study of archetypal ideas and scientific theories, reflecting a dialogue between psychology and physics.
Jung's proposal raises an ontological question about whether all significant relations must be reducible to ordinary causal chains.
The concept remains interpretive and controversial and should not be coded as an established physical law of acausal influence.
Meaningful coincidence is different from demonstrating a hidden causal mechanism or nonlocal signal transfer.
Rigorous extraction should separate reported coincidences, statistical discussion and Jung's metaphysical interpretation.
The Dhammasangani enumerates ultimate phenomena or dhammas used within the Abhidhamma analytical framework.
The text classifies many possible states of consciousness (citta) as part of a systematic analysis of mind.
Mental factors (cetasikas) are analyzed in combinations that accompany different states of consciousness.
The analytical framework focuses on processes and constituent phenomena rather than positing a permanent soul as an explanatory unit.
States of mind are distinguished partly by wholesome, unwholesome and ethically indeterminate qualities.
Mental activity is analyzed through constituent factors, supporting a fine-grained model of how particular states arise.
The Abhidhamma project links mental states to conditional relations among phenomena rather than a single enduring self.
Mental events are treated as conditioned and changing rather than as a permanently fixed state.
The larger Abhidhamma system distinguishes mental phenomena from physical phenomena while analyzing their relations.
The analytical taxonomy supports a broader Buddhist project of understanding conditions that sustain suffering and those associated with liberation.
Detailed classification of mental states provides a systematic vocabulary for describing varieties of experience and cognition.
Dhammasangani belongs to a religious-philosophical analytical tradition and should not be equated directly with modern experimental psychology.
The source is valuable for comparing process-based analyses of mind, attention and selflessness with contemporary models while preserving doctrinal context.
Huayan interpretations of the Avatamsaka describe phenomena as mutually interpenetrating rather than existing as fully isolated entities.
The imagery of Indra's net represents a universe in which each jewel reflects all the others without abolishing their distinctness.
The whole is presented as dynamically related to every part, providing a radical model of relational unity.
The sutra links awakening, mind and the structure of reality within a Mahayana Buddhist framework.
Ordinary distinctions are not simply denied but are reinterpreted within a larger non-dual or mutually conditioning perspective.
The bodhisattva path places compassion, wisdom and practice at the center of transformation toward awakening.
How phenomena are apprehended is transformed by insight into their interdependence and emptiness.
The framework undermines an isolated substantial self by emphasizing relational arising and mutual dependence.
Long temporal scales and vast cosmological sequences are used to depict the scope of bodhisattva practice and awakening.
The text uses an expansive cosmological vision in which many realms and beings participate in an interconnected order.
Practice is expressed through conduct, vows and compassion rather than as a purely abstract intellectual doctrine.
Huayan cosmological and ontological claims belong to Buddhist scripture and interpretation, not to established physical cosmology.
For comparative work, interpenetration, emptiness, compassion and cosmology should be distinguished from later metaphysical or scientific analogies.
The Qingjing tradition presents purity and clarity of mind as central conditions of spiritual cultivation.
Stillness or tranquility is treated as a practice for reducing agitation and returning the mind toward a simpler condition.
Attachment and desire are depicted as forces that disturb clarity and contribute to inner disorder.
The text frames spiritual cultivation in terms of regulating and clarifying the mind rather than accumulating conceptual knowledge.
The human path is oriented toward alignment with Dao through purification and tranquility.
Daoist cultivation links mental quieting with embodied practice and the condition of the living organism.
Release from excessive grasping supports a less reified relation to self and phenomena.
The scripture situates personal cultivation within a larger Daoist account of Heaven, Earth and the natural order.
Purity is connected with conduct and the reduction of actions driven by disruptive desires.
Regular cultivation is presented as a transformation of the practitioner's state rather than a purely intellectual belief.
The scripture is a Daoist religious text and its cosmological claims should not be rewritten as empirical scientific propositions.
The Chinese Text Project notes that the text occurs in the Yunji Qiqian and in the Daozang tradition, and that its textual history has multiple related versions.
The source is useful for coding stillness, desire, mind cultivation and Dao alignment as a coherent contemplative pathway.
The Menog i Khrad belongs to the Middle Persian wisdom literature concerned with human conduct, wisdom and religious understanding.
The tradition links ethical and spiritual development with the condition and destiny of the soul.
Self-knowledge is treated as important for understanding one's origins, religious identity and ultimate end.
Zoroastrian ethics emphasizes the integrated triad of good thought, good word and good action.
Moral character is assessed through the consequences and quality of thoughts, words and deeds.
Education and learning are presented as routes toward wisdom and better conduct.
Association with wise and good people is treated as a support for religious and ethical development.
The soul of the righteous is described within a theological framework relating human goodness to divine reality.
The ethical life is linked with happiness, reward and the ultimate condition of the person.
Cultivating correct thought, speech and action is presented as a path of moral transformation.
The Menog i Khrad is a religious wisdom text, so theological claims about soul and divine order must remain within their historical doctrinal context.
Its threefold ethical framework is distinct from a modern neural or computational theory of consciousness, even though both can be compared at the level of self-regulation and action.
Comparative extraction should preserve the original ethical vocabulary rather than retrofitting it into contemporary psychological categories.
Sefer ha-Razim is an early Jewish magical text organized around heavenly realms, angels and ritual knowledge.
The reconstructed text is organized into seven heavenly or firmamental sections associated with different beings and powers.
Angels and other supernatural beings are invoked as intermediaries within the ritual system of the text.
The text includes formulas and procedures aimed at gaining knowledge, protection or access to supernatural information.
The text presupposes a religious cosmology in which human persons interact with powers beyond ordinary physical experience.
Knowledge in the text is not merely theoretical; it is tied to prescribed words, names and ritual actions.
Cambridge's account identifies Mordecai Margalioth's reconstruction and Michael A. Morgan's translation and annotation as important modern transmission points.
The surviving material represents an early Jewish magical tradition from the first centuries of the Common Era.
The heavens are arranged as a structured hierarchy with differentiated inhabitants and powers.
The text treats special knowledge as obtainable through ritual access to hidden or heavenly realities.
These supernatural claims belong to the text's religious-magical worldview and are not empirical claims established by modern science.
Sefer ha-Razim should not be conflated with later Jewish mystical systems simply because both discuss hidden heavenly realities.
For corpus purposes, manuscript reconstruction, translation history, ritual description and theological interpretation should be kept separately coded.
Mawaqif is structured around spiritual 'stoppings' or stations in which the seeker encounters divine disclosure.
The text presents episodes of encounter with divine reality through a highly compressed mystical idiom.
The qalb/heart functions as a key locus of spiritual perception and transformation in the Sufi vocabulary associated with the work.
Nafs-related language frames the disciplined self whose ordinary tendencies can obstruct direct spiritual realization.
The rūḥ vocabulary points toward a deeper spiritual dimension beyond ordinary ego identity.
Ma'rifa or direct spiritual knowing is presented as distinct from merely discursive or propositional knowledge.
The stations are transformative encounters that alter the seeker's relation to self, world and God.
The language frequently compresses subject-object distinctions in describing divine presence and realization.
The seeker is called toward sustained inward attention and receptivity to disclosure.
Spiritual realization is not isolated from discipline, surrender and transformation of the self.
The text belongs to Islamic mystical literature and should not be converted into a neuroscience claim merely because it describes altered states or direct knowing.
Exact terminology and source relationships require critical-edition verification before fine-grained historical claims are made.
Until the register's exact edition is recovered, C323 should remain a corpus-level, source-attributed extraction rather than a fully bibliographically resolved one.
